chapter.name: Pressure, Winds, Storms, and Cyclones
chapter.blurb: Starting from why a bag with narrow straps hurts more than one with broad straps, the chapter builds up the idea of pressure as force per unit area, shows that liquids and the air around us also exert pressure, explains how differences in air pressure create wind, sea breezes and land breezes, and uses the same idea of pressure to explain storms, thunderstorms, lightning and cyclones, ending with how to stay safe during them.

scope_in.item: Pressure as force per unit area, its SI unit newton per square metre (pascal, Pa), and the formula Pressure = Force / Area, including a worked numeric example (100 N over 2 square metres)
Why broad straps, bucket handles and head-load pads reduce pressure, and why a pointed nail or a knife's sharp edge is easier to use than its blunt side, all by changing the area a force acts over

Liquids exert pressure that increases with the height of the liquid column, and exert pressure in all directions, including on the sides of a container (the balloon-and-pipe and leaking-bottle activities); why a dam's base is built broader than its top

In vessels filled to the same height, the pressure at the bottom is equal regardless of shape, though the total force on the base can differ if the base areas differ (an extension drawn from the end-of-chapter exercises)

The atmosphere and its rough composition (nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide); that air exerts pressure in all directions, shown by the paper-plate-and-chart-paper activity, an inflating balloon, and a rubber sucker sticking to a surface
The approximate magnitude of atmospheric pressure, why our bodies are not crushed by it, and the units pascal (N/m2), millibar (mb) and hectopascal (hPa), including conversions between them
Air/wind flows from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure (the balloon-and-straw activity), and how this explains sea breeze during the day and land breeze at night

High-speed winds are accompanied by a lowering of air pressure (the two-balloon blowing activity); why weak roofs may be blown off in a storm, why keeping doors and windows open during a storm reduces this risk, and why holes are cut in banners and hoardings (drawn from the end-of-chapter exercises)
Formation of a storm: warm moist air rising, condensation forming clouds and rain, hail or snow, and why storms are more frequent in hot, humid, tropical regions like India

How strong up-and-down winds inside storm clouds separate electric charge, how the resulting discharge produces lightning (within a cloud, between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground), how lightning produces thunder, and the regional names Kalboishakhi, Bordoisila and mango showers for local pre-monsoon thunderstorms
Lightning safety precautions and how a lightning conductor protects a building

How a cyclone forms over warm ocean water, including the role of condensation, rising air and the Earth's rotation; the eye of a cyclone and the surrounding strong winds and heavy rain; why a cyclone weakens over land

The destructive effects of cyclones (storm surge, flooding, landslides, contaminated water and farmland, blocked roads, power outages) and how forecasting, warnings, emergency kits and cyclone shelters help protect people

concepts.name: Pressure: force spread over an area
concepts.description: Pressure is introduced as the force acting on each unit of area, using the story of two identical bags with different strap widths, and applied to everyday examples like knives, nails and bucket handles.
concepts.idea: Pressure is the force acting per unit area, and spreading the same force over a larger area makes the pressure smaller.
concepts.rule: Megha and Pawan carry identical, equally heavy bags to a picnic, but Pawan's bag with narrow straps hurts his shoulders while Megha's bag with broad straps does not. The weight of a bag acts on the shoulder because of gravity, but narrow straps spread this force over a smaller area of the shoulder, while broad straps spread the same force over a larger area. Since the area over which a force acts matters, we define pressure as force per unit area: Pressure = Force / Area. At this stage, only forces acting perpendicular to the surface are considered. The SI unit of force is the newton and of area the square metre, so the SI unit of pressure is newton per square metre (N/m2), also called the pascal (Pa). For example, a force of 100 N spread over an area of 2 square metres gives a pressure of 100 N / 2 m2 = 50 N/m2. The same idea explains why it is easier to lift a bucket by a broad handle than a narrow one, why people carrying loads on their heads use a round cloth pad, why it is easier to drive a nail in using its pointed end rather than its head, and why a knife's sharp edge cuts more easily than its blunt edge: in every case, concentrating the same force on a smaller area produces a much greater pressure.
concepts.example: A force of 100 newtons spread over an area of 2 square metres gives a pressure of 50 newtons per square metre (50 pascals).

questions.q: Design one everyday object, other than those mentioned in the chapter, that works by increasing or decreasing pressure through changing area. Explain how it works.

concepts.name: Liquid pressure: depends on height, acts in all directions
concepts.description: Two activities with balloons, pipes and a leaking bottle show that liquids exert pressure that grows with the height of the liquid column and pushes outward in every direction, which also explains why a dam's base is broader than its top.
concepts.idea: Liquids exert pressure in all directions, and the pressure at any point depends on the height of the liquid column above it, not on the shape of the container.
concepts.rule: In Activity 6.1, two transparent pipes of different diameters, each with a balloon tied to one end, are filled with water to the same height; both balloons bulge to the same extent, showing that the amount of water does not decide the bulge, but the height of the water column does. Adding more water and raising the column further makes the balloon bulge more, so liquid pressure increases with the height of the column, and is why overhead tanks are placed at a height, to increase the pressure at the taps below. In Activity 6.2, a bottle with holes made at the same height all around it, when filled with water, lets water spurt out equally from every hole, showing that liquids exert pressure not only downward but also sideways, in fact in all directions. This is also why the base of a dam is built much broader than its top: the water pressure that acts horizontally on the dam wall is largest near the bottom, so a broad base is needed to withstand it. Since pressure depends only on the height of a liquid column and not on the container's shape, two vessels filled with water to the same height have equal pressure at their base; however, since force equals pressure multiplied by area, a vessel with a larger base area experiences a greater total force even though the pressure is the same.
concepts.example: Two glass pipes of different width filled with water to the same height produce equally bulging balloons at the bottom, because liquid pressure depends only on the height of the column, not on the pipe's width.

concepts.name: Atmospheric pressure: air exerts pressure too
concepts.description: The paper-plate, balloon and rubber-sucker activities show that the air of the atmosphere presses on everything around us in all directions, and this atmospheric pressure can be measured in pascals, millibars or hectopascals.
concepts.idea: The air of the atmosphere presses on everything around us in all directions, and this atmospheric pressure can be measured in pascals, millibars or hectopascals.
concepts.rule: The envelope of air surrounding the Earth is called the atmosphere, made up mostly of nitrogen and oxygen, with smaller amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and other gases, and extending many kilometres above the Earth's surface. In Activity 6.3, lifting a paper plate covered with an unfolded chart paper sheet takes more effort than lifting it covered with a folded sheet of the same weight, because the unfolded sheet has a larger area, so the same atmospheric pressure produces a bigger downward force on it; this shows that air exerts pressure. A balloon inflates and expands in all directions because the air inside it exerts pressure equally on every part of its walls. In Activity 6.4, a rubber sucker pressed onto a flat surface sticks firmly because pressing it out removes most of the air between the sucker and the surface, lowering the pressure inside it; the higher atmospheric pressure outside then holds the sucker against the surface. The force of the atmosphere on an area of just 15 cm x 15 cm is nearly equal to the weight of a 225 kg object (about 2250 N), yet we are not crushed because the pressure inside our own body, caused by the fluids and gases in our tissues and organs, balances the atmospheric pressure pushing in from outside. Besides the pascal (N/m2), air pressure is also measured in millibar (mb), where 1 mb = 100 Pa, and hectopascal (hPa), where 1 hPa = 100 Pa.
concepts.example: The force of the atmosphere on a 15 cm by 15 cm patch of surface is about the same as the weight of a 225 kg object, yet we are not crushed because the pressure inside our bodies balances it.

questions.q: Design a simple way to demonstrate to a younger student that air exerts pressure, without using a rubber sucker or the paper-plate activity from the chapter.

concepts.name: Wind formation and how speed affects pressure
concepts.description: Two balloon activities show that air always flows from high pressure to low pressure, that this explains sea and land breezes, and that faster-moving air is itself at a lower pressure, which explains why storms can blow off weak roofs.
concepts.idea: Air flows from regions of high pressure to regions of low pressure, and this flowing air is wind; faster-moving air is itself at a lower pressure.
concepts.rule: In Activity 6.5, a straw connects an inflated balloon to an uninflated one; air moves through the straw from the inflated (higher-pressure) balloon into the uninflated (lower-pressure) balloon until both balloons are almost the same size and the airflow stops, showing that air moves from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure. This same idea explains sea and land breezes: during the day, land heats up faster than water, so the warm air above the land rises and creates a low-pressure area there, and air from the higher-pressure sea flows in to replace it, giving a sea breeze; at night, the sea stays warmer than the land, so a low-pressure area forms over the sea instead, and wind blows from the land to the sea, giving a land breeze. In Activity 6.6, blowing air into the narrow gap between two balloons hung close together makes them move towards each other, and blowing harder makes them approach faster; this happens because the fast-moving air between the balloons is itself at a lower pressure, so the higher pressure surrounding them pushes them inward, showing that high-speed winds are accompanied by a reduced air pressure. During a storm, high-speed winds blowing over a roof create a low-pressure area above it, so if the pressure difference between inside the house and above the roof becomes large and the roof is weak, it may be blown off; keeping doors and windows open during a storm lets air move through the house, reducing this pressure difference and helping protect the roof. Holes are similarly cut into large banners and hoardings to let wind pass through them, reducing the force that could tear them or blow them away.

concepts.name: Storms, thunderstorms and lightning
concepts.description: Warm moist air rising and cooling explains how storms and their rain, hail or snow form, and strong up-and-down winds inside the clouds go on to separate electric charge, producing lightning and thunder.
concepts.idea: A storm is strong wind with rain, and when strong up-and-down winds inside a storm separate electric charges in the clouds, the sudden discharge produces lightning and thunder.
concepts.rule: When land gets heated, the warm, moist air above it, being lighter, rises and creates a low-pressure area; cooler air from surrounding higher-pressure areas flows in to take its place, gets heated in turn, and also rises, setting up a continuous cycle of wind circulation. As the rising air expands, it cools, and the moisture in it condenses to form water droplets, creating clouds; the droplets merge into heavier drops that fall as rain, hail or snow. Strong winds accompanied by rain make up a storm, and storms are more frequent in hot, humid, tropical regions like India. Strong winds blowing both upwards and downwards inside the cloud cause water droplets and ice particles to rub against each other, building up static electric charge; the lighter, positively charged ice particles rise to occupy the upper part of the cloud, while the heavier, negatively charged water droplets occupy the lower part, so a charge separation forms within the cloud. Air normally acts as an electrical insulator, keeping opposite charges apart, but once the build-up of charge becomes very large, the insulating property of the air breaks down, and a sudden flow of charge produces a bright flash of light called lightning, which can occur within a cloud, between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground. Lightning rapidly heats the air around it, making it expand suddenly and produce the loud sound called thunder; a storm accompanied by lightning and thunder is a thunderstorm. Local pre-monsoon thunderstorms are known by regional names: Kalboishakhi in West Bengal, Bihar and Jharkhand, and Bordoisila in Assam, both helping kharif crops to grow, while in Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu they are called mango showers, supporting the ripening of mangoes, and in Karnataka they also help coffee plants grow. Since lightning can be dangerous, during a storm one should stay away from tall objects, find a low-lying open area and crouch down, avoid lying down flat, avoid a metal-rod umbrella, get out of water if in it, and note that a bus or car is comparatively safer. A lightning conductor, a metallic rod with one pointed end kept higher than the building and its other end buried deep in the ground, provides an easy path for electric charge to travel safely into the ground, protecting the building.

concepts.name: Cyclones: formation, structure and protection
concepts.description: Warm ocean water, condensation and the Earth's rotation combine to build a cyclone, a spinning system of clouds, wind and rain with a calm eye at its centre and highly destructive winds and flooding around it.
concepts.idea: A cyclone is a large spinning system of clouds, wind and rain that forms over warm ocean water, with a calm low-pressure eye at its centre and violent winds around it.
concepts.rule: Cyclones are large storms that form over warm ocean waters. As the ocean water heats up, the warm, moist air above it rises; as this moist air rises, its water vapour condenses to form raindrops, and since condensation releases the heat that evaporation had earlier taken up, this warms the rising air further, making it rise even more and creating an even lower pressure. Air from the surrounding regions rushes in to fill this low-pressure area and also starts rising, and the Earth's rotation causes this moving air to spin; the cycle repeats, building a very low-pressure area with high-speed winds revolving around it, which is a cyclone. The region of lowest pressure sits at the very centre, called the eye of the cyclone, where the wind is calm, while the surrounding region experiences strong winds and heavy rainfall; as a cyclone moves from the ocean towards land it generates higher wind speeds than ordinary thunderstorms, but once it reaches land, its source of moist air is cut off and it gradually loses strength. Cyclones can be extremely destructive: the Amphan cyclone of 2020, for example, had peak wind speeds of 270 km/h. Strong winds during a cyclone push ocean water towards the shore, creating a storm surge, a wall of water as high as 3 to 12 metres, that can flood coastal areas and even areas further inland; heavy rainfall can make rivers overflow and trigger landslides, seawater rushing inland can contaminate drinking water and make farmland soil less fertile because of its salt, fallen trees and debris can block roads, and power outages can disrupt emergency services and daily life for days. Protection relies on staying updated with alerts and warnings from the India Meteorological Department (IMD), using weather satellites to track cyclones and predict their path, keeping an emergency kit ready in cyclone-prone areas, and moving quickly to a nearby designated cyclone shelter when a cyclone approaches.
